about: Identifying features of prehistoric animals, written from museum and encyclopedia descriptions opened on 2026-10-06. Used to word each animal's prompt and to check each tile feature by feature. 'disagreement' is the researcher's full note; plan.json carries only the part that changes how the animal looks.

animals.name: Brachiosaurus
features: Front legs longer than back legs, so shoulders stand much higher than hips and the back slopes down toward the tail.
Giraffe-like build: very long neck leaving the shoulders at a steep upward angle, held high in a gentle S-curve.
Deep chest and large body carried on four slender, straight, column-like legs; always on all fours.
Small head, tall in profile, with a long blunt snout; nostrils drawn at the front of the snout.
Tail muscular but noticeably short for a sauropod.
Roughly 18-22 m long with the head 9-13 m above ground; an adult person stands well below its belly.
Probably a small hump over the shoulders where the neck muscles attach.
not_this: Nostrils on top of the head, or the animal standing deep in water using its head as a snorkel (old swamp idea).
Rearing up on its hind legs as in films; its weight sat too far forward for that.
A level back with front and back legs the same length.
animals.tell_apart: The only one of the four whose front legs are longer than its back legs: shoulders well above hips, back sloping down to a short tail, neck rising steeply like a giraffe's. Diplodocus and Brontosaurus have a level back, a lower neck and a very long whip tail. Argentinosaurus is far bigger and broader and should not be given the high-shouldered slope.
animals.disagreement: NHM notes there is no complete skeleton and most full-body reconstructions borrow from the African Giraffatitan. Wikipedia reports ongoing debate on neck posture, from near-vertical to horizontal, with the raised giraffe-like pose best supported for this animal; height estimates range from 9.4 to 13 m.

animals.name: Brontosaurus
features: Heavily built sauropod on four thick, straight legs; front legs slightly shorter than back legs, back arching highest over the hips.
Long neck that is strikingly thick, wide and deep, about twice as massive as the neck of other diplodocids.
Very small, low head with a squared-off snout, like the head of Diplodocus.
Tail over half the total length, tapering to a thin whip and carried in the air.
Each front foot shows one large inward-pointing claw; the other front toes have no claws.
About 21-23 m long and 4.5 m tall at the back; an adult person stands under half that height.
Walking on dry land with legs upright beneath the body, hind legs bending in a stride.
not_this: Tail dragging on the ground (old museum mounts and books).
A short, tall, boxy head; early skeletons wore a wrong Camarasaurus-style skull.
Standing half-sunk in a swamp or lake to support its weight.
animals.tell_apart: Same layout as Diplodocus (level back, whip tail, small low head) but visibly stockier: a thick, deep, wide neck, heavier legs and body, and shorter overall (about 22 m against 26 m). Unlike Brachiosaurus its shoulders are not above its hips and its neck does not rise steeply. Far smaller and less massive than Argentinosaurus.
animals.disagreement: The AMNH OLogy card still treats Brontosaurus as the same animal as Apatosaurus and calls the name 'extinct'; Wikipedia, Britannica and Yale follow the 2015 study that revived the genus, which not all palaeontologists accept. No skull has been found (it is drawn from Apatosaurus), and neck posture is debated between roughly level and raised.

animals.name: Diplodocus
features: Very long, slim sauropod, about 24-26 m, lightly built for its length.
Front legs slightly shorter than back legs, giving a largely horizontal body.
Long slender neck held roughly level or gently raised, not straight up.
Extremely long tail, over half the total length, tapering to a thin whip and balancing the neck.
Very small, low head; peg-like teeth only at the front of the mouth, pointing forward.
May show a row of narrow pointed spines along the tail, back and neck, like an iguana's.
Skin of small pebbly scales; front feet are compact columns with one large thumb claw each.
not_this: Legs sprawled out sideways like a lizard with the belly near the ground (reconstructions from about 1910).
Tail dragging along the ground.
Wading or swimming in deep water as a swamp animal.
animals.tell_apart: The slimmest and longest-looking of the four: thin neck, light body, level back, whip tail, and optionally a row of small spines. Brontosaurus has the same layout but is clearly stockier with a much thicker, deeper neck. Brachiosaurus has high shoulders, a sloping back and a short tail. Argentinosaurus is far bulkier and broader, with no whip tail or spines.
animals.disagreement: NHM says ligaments held the neck horizontal, while Wikipedia also reports a 2009 study arguing sauropods habitually raised the base of the neck. NHM calls the back spines 'bony' but Wikipedia calls them keratinous and notes the spine-bearing skin fossils may belong to a close relative; no definite Diplodocus skull is known.

animals.name: Argentinosaurus
features: Gigantic four-legged sauropod about 30-35 m long; an adult person stands only about knee-high beside it.
Extremely massive, deep-bodied and wide-hipped (about 65-80 tonnes), far heavier-looking than a Diplodocus of similar length.
Four straight, column-like legs under the body; back legs about 4.5 m tall, thigh bone alone 2.5 m.
Long neck with a small head, restored from related titanosaurs; no neck bones or skull have been found.
Long tapering tail, also restored from relatives; no tail bones have been found.
Shoulders about 7 m above ground in the museum's mounted skeleton reconstruction.
Plain skin with no crest, sail, spines or armour; none is known for this animal.
not_this: Invented details shown as fact: a head crest, back spines, armour plates or a whip tail have no fossil support.
A high-shouldered giraffe shape copied from Brachiosaurus.
Tail dragging on the ground, or the animal wading in a swamp.
animals.tell_apart: Distinguish it mainly by sheer size and bulk: include a scale cue (trees, a person, another dinosaur) and draw a broad, very heavy body with a thick neck. Unlike Brachiosaurus, do not put the shoulders far above the hips; unlike Diplodocus and Brontosaurus, no thin whip tail and no spines. These proportions come from related titanosaurs, not from Argentinosaurus bones.
animals.disagreement: KNOWN: seven back vertebrae, the underside of the fused hip vertebrae with some hip ribs, part of one rib and a 1.55 m calf bone; two 2.5 m thigh bones are assigned to it with doubt. RECONSTRUCTED from related titanosaurs: head, neck, tail, front legs, feet and skin. Estimates vary: NHM gives 35 m and 70 tonnes, Wikipedia cites 30 to nearly 40 m and 50-100 tonnes, and whether it or Patagotitan was larger is disputed.

animals.name: Amargasaurus
features: Small sauropod about 9-13 m long and 2.5 m high, with a barrel-shaped body on four column-like legs.
Neck short for a sauropod, about 2.4 m, carried low or gently sloping, never upright.
Two parallel rows of tall, thin, tapering spines along the neck, tallest mid-neck at about 60 cm, curving backward.
The paired spines continue, shorter, onto the front of the back.
Over the hips and tail base, a single row of paddle-shaped spines makes a low ridge.
Small head with a broad, horse-like snout and pencil-like teeth, pointing downward.
Front legs somewhat shorter than back legs; long tapering tail.
Spines either joined by skin into a neck sail or shown as separate horn-covered spikes.
not_this: One tall sail down the middle of the back, like Spinosaurus or Dimetrodon.
A long neck raised upright like a giraffe's; the spines stopped it lifting the neck vertically.
A smooth neck with no spines, or only a single row of spines on the neck.
animals.tell_apart: The only sauropod in the game with spines: a double row of tall spines (or a sail) on a short neck. It is also by far the smallest, about 10 m, while the other four are two to three times longer and have smooth necks.
animals.disagreement: Both sources leave open whether the spines carried a skin sail or were separate horn-sheathed spikes; Wikipedia cites a 2022 bone study favouring a sail joined by ligaments, against earlier work favouring spikes. Only the back of the skull is known, so the snout is restored from relatives. (The NHM Dino Directory page for this animal returned a server error, so the Western Australian Museum page was used as the museum source.)

animals.name: Pachycephalosaurus
features: Walks on two long, strong back legs; heavy tail held stiff and straight out behind, off the ground.
Large, smooth, rounded bony dome on top of the head (bone up to 25 cm thick).
Bony knobs edge the back of the dome; short, blunt spikes point up from the snout.
Short skull with a small muzzle ending in a pointed beak; large round eyes facing forward.
Short arms with five-fingered hands, a bulky body, and a fairly short, thick neck.
About 3-4.5 m long and 370-450 kg; roughly car-length, not a giant.
not_this: Upright kangaroo pose with the tail resting or dragging on the ground.
Long sharp horns; adults had short blunt knobs and spikes (long horns belong to young animals once named Stygimoloch).
A flat head with no dome (the juvenile form once named Dracorex).
animals.tell_apart: No look-alike among these eleven: it is the only two-legged animal here, with a short neck and a domed head ringed by knobs. It is not a long-necked sauropod and has no wings.
animals.disagreement: NHM gives a length of 3 m, Wikipedia about 4.5 m. Wikipedia says only skull remains are described, so the body is reconstructed from related dome-headed dinosaurs, and that the flat-headed, long-spiked Dracorex and Stygimoloch are now widely seen as young Pachycephalosaurus.

animals.name: Pterodactylus
features: Small pterosaur: wingspan about 1 m (at most 1.5 m), far smaller than a person.
Long, thin, straight jaws with about 90 small cone-shaped teeth, largest at the jaw tips.
Short tail, barely visible; no long tail and no tail vane.
Low soft crest on top of the head, small and triangular with its peak above the eyes.
Possibly a small flexible tab sticking back from the rear of the skull.
Wing is skin stretched from one very long fourth finger back to the hind leg; three small clawed fingers stay free.
Short hair-like fuzz on head and body; wing membranes bare.
On the ground it walks on all fours with the outer wings folded up.
not_this: Huge size, a toothless beak or a long bony crest pointing backward: that is Pteranodon.
A long tail with a diamond tip: that is Rhamphorhynchus.
Bat wings with several fingers in the membrane, bare scaly skin, or standing upright on two legs.
animals.tell_apart: Pteranodon is about six times larger, has no teeth at all and carries a big bony crest sweeping back from the skull; Pterodactylus is small, has a mouth full of small teeth and only a low soft crest above the eyes. Unlike Rhamphorhynchus and Dimorphodon its tail is a short stub. Unlike Quetzalcoatlus it is tiny, toothed and short-necked by comparison.
animals.disagreement: Wingspan differs by source: Wikipedia about 1.04 m from the single adult skull, AMNH up to 1.5 m, Britannica 50 cm to over 1 m. Wikipedia notes dispute over whether the soft crest and rear skull tab extended behind the head and whether those fossils are Pterodactylus at all; Britannica says some pterosaurs walked on two legs, while AMNH and Wikipedia say trackways show four-limbed walking.

animals.name: Pteranodon
features: Very large: adult male wingspan about 5.6-7 m, several times a person's height; females about 3.8 m.
Long, slender, completely toothless beak ending in a sharp point; upper jaw slightly longer and gently upturned.
Bony crest rising from the back of the skull and sweeping backward: long and blade-like in males, short and rounded in females.
Small body, about turkey-sized, between long narrow albatross-like wings.
Very short tail, about 25 cm at most, hardly visible.
Wing is skin stretched from one hugely long fourth finger; three small clawed fingers at the wing's front edge.
Fuzzy, hair-like body covering rather than scales or feathers.
If on the ground, it stands on all fours with wings folded.
not_this: Teeth in the beak, as some film and toy versions show.
Carrying off people or large animals in its feet; it weighed only about 20-50 kg and ate fish.
A long tail, bat-like wings, or perching upright on two legs like a bird.
animals.tell_apart: Against Pterodactylus: far bigger, no teeth, and a long bony crest pointing backward instead of a low soft crest. Against Quetzalcoatlus: shorter neck, long backswept crest, long narrow seabird wings and a small body, whereas Quetzalcoatlus has a very long neck, long legs and stands giraffe-tall. Against Rhamphorhynchus and Dimorphodon: no long tail and no teeth.
animals.disagreement: Wingspan figures differ: Field Museum 18 ft, AMNH up to 20 ft (6 m), Britannica 7 m or more, Wikipedia 5.6 m for an average male with the largest over 7 m. Crest shape depends on sex and species (upright in P. sternbergi, backswept in P. longiceps), and Britannica allows two-legged walking in some pterosaurs while Wikipedia says trackways point to four limbs.

animals.name: Quetzalcoatlus
features: Gigantic: wingspan about 10-11 m, as wide as a small aeroplane.
Standing on all fours it is giraffe-tall: shoulders about 2.5-3 m, head 4-5 m above ground.
Very long, straight neck, up to about 3 m, carried upward like a giraffe's.
Huge head with a long, slender, pointed, toothless beak, far longer than the small body.
Small crest on top of the skull at the base of the beak; exact shape unknown (squarish or rounded).
Small torso; long legs and folded wing-arms held straight beneath the body when walking.
Hair-like fuzz on the body; wing membrane runs from the wing-finger tip to the ankle.
Tail tiny or not visible.
not_this: Teeth, or a long backward-pointing Pteranodon-style crest.
A short neck, or perching upright on two legs with wings spread.
Bare scaly or leathery dragon skin, or feathers.
animals.tell_apart: Against Pteranodon: much larger, with a very long stiff neck, long stork-like legs and only a small crest near the beak base, and on the ground it stands as tall as a giraffe. Against Pterodactylus: enormously larger and toothless. Against Rhamphorhynchus and Dimorphodon: no long tail, no teeth, giant size.
animals.disagreement: AMNH and Britannica give a standing height of about 5 m, while NHM and Wikipedia put the shoulders at 2.5-3 m with the head over 4 m; AMNH calls the wings long and thin, Wikipedia short and broad. The giant species is known mainly from wing bones (AMNH: 'parts of one wing'), so its head, neck and legs are scaled up from the smaller Q. lawsoni, whose crest shape and beak tip are not preserved.

animals.name: Rhamphorhynchus
features: Small: wingspan usually about 1 m, at most 1.8 m; body about 50 cm long, hawk-sized.
Long, thin, stiff tail ending in a flat diamond-shaped vane, like a kite's tail.
Long, low skull with needle-like teeth slanting forward and interlocking when the jaws close.
Jaw tips toothless, sharp and beak-like; the lower jaw tip hooks slightly upward.
No crest of any kind on the head; large eyes.
Short body and short legs; thin wing membranes stretched from the long fourth finger to the hind legs.
Probable hair-like fuzz on the body; wing membranes bare.
not_this: A short tail, or a long tail with no diamond vane at the tip.
Any head crest (an old report of one was shown to be a mistake).
A toothless beak, or neat upright teeth; the teeth must jut forward.
animals.tell_apart: Against Dimorphodon: Rhamphorhynchus has a slim, low head with forward-slanting needle teeth and a clear diamond vane on the tail tip; Dimorphodon has a big, deep head, front fangs with tiny teeth behind, shorter wings and no confirmed vane. Against the short-tailed Pterodactylus, Pteranodon and Quetzalcoatlus: a long stiff tail with a vane and no crest.
animals.disagreement: Britannica gives a wingspan of about 1 m, while AMNH, NHM and Wikipedia give up to 1.8 m for the largest adults. Wikipedia says the tail vane changed with age (oval in the young, diamond in adults, triangular in the largest), so a diamond suits a typical adult.

animals.name: Dimorphodon
features: Small and stocky: about 1 m long with a wingspan of about 1.4 m.
Very large, deep head, about 23 cm long, big for the body, with large eyes.
Two kinds of teeth: four or five long fangs at the front of each jaw, many tiny teeth behind.
Short, strong neck.
Long, stiff, straight tail of about 30 bones; a small vane at the tip is optional, none has been found.
Wings short for its body; three free fingers with large curved claws on each wing.
On the ground it goes on all fours with wings folded like an umbrella; a good climber.
not_this: Running upright on two legs like a little dinosaur (older reconstructions).
A smooth puffin-style beak hiding the teeth; that beak is speculation and the fangs must show.
A short tail, a head crest, or long narrow seabird wings.
animals.tell_apart: Against Rhamphorhynchus: Dimorphodon's head is big and deep (tall as well as long) with a few front fangs and tiny back teeth, its wings are short and its build stocky; Rhamphorhynchus has a slim low head, forward-slanting needle teeth and a diamond tail vane. Against the short-tailed Pterodactylus, Pteranodon and Quetzalcoatlus: a long stiff tail, a deep toothy head and no crest.
animals.disagreement: Britannica says it 'probably walked on two legs', while Wikipedia and AMNH say trackways and computer modelling show pterosaurs, including Dimorphodon, walked on four limbs. Wingspan differs (AMNH 1.4 m, Wikipedia 1.45 m, Britannica 1.7 m), and AMNH describes a flap on the tail end although Wikipedia says no vane impression has been found.
